title: A line from artificial atom 1

Which wavelength is emitted? Use $h=6.63\times10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s}$, $c=3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $1\,\mathrm{eV}=1.60\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$.

verification.method: author reasoning, conservation and deterministic numerical checks
verification.notes: Skill family: E1-F2 emission transitions in constructed atomic levels. Variant 1 of 4. Original constructed context/data and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, assumptions and allocations; not independent exam moderation.

steps.text: Option D. The photon carries the positive energy difference $5.6-2.2=3.4\,\mathrm{eV}$. Hence $\lambda=hc/\Delta E=366\,\mathrm{nm}$. Using a level energy rather than the difference describes a different transition.

title: Nuclear size model for A = 27
stem: Approximate a nucleus of nucleon number $27$ as a uniform sphere. Use $R=r_0A^{1/3}$, with $r_0=1.20\times10^{-15}\,\mathrm{m}$, and a mass of $1.66\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$ per nucleon. Ignore the mass defect for this size model.

verification.method: author reasoning, conservation and deterministic numerical checks
verification.notes: Skill family: E1-F3 nuclear radius scaling and density. Variant 1 of 4. Original constructed context/data and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, assumptions and allocations; not independent exam moderation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the nuclear radius.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Estimate the nuclear mass density.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why this model predicts approximately the same density for a nucleus with eight times as many nucleons.

steps.text: $\rho=A m_u/(\frac43\pi R^3)$, with $m=4.48\times10^{-26}\,\mathrm{kg}$.
$\rho=2.29\times10^{17}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$. Accept consistent error carried forward from the radius.
Eight times as many nucleons give twice the radius and eight times the volume.
Mass and volume increase by the same factor, leaving density unchanged.

subject: physics-hl
title: Testing a nuclear size bound 1
stem: An alpha particle of charge $+2e$ approaches a nucleus of charge $+29e$ head-on from very far away with kinetic energy $4.00\,\mathrm{MeV}$. Ignore recoil and electron screening. Use $k=8.99\times10^9\,\mathrm{N\,m^2\,C^{-2}}$ and $e=1.60\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$. The estimated nuclear radius is $4.00\,\mathrm{fm}$.

verification.method: author reasoning, conservation and deterministic numerical checks
verification.notes: Skill family: E1-F4 closest approach and finite nuclear size. Variant 1 of 4. Original constructed context/data and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, assumptions and allocations; not independent exam moderation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the closest distance between the two centres in the point-charge model.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Estimate the incident energy that would make the model's closest approach equal to the given nuclear radius.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Assess the model for the original incident energy and explain why the second result is not a precise prediction of a nuclear collision.

steps.text: At the turning point, kinetic energy is zero; conserve energy using $E_k=k(2e)(Ze)/r$.
Convert the incident energy to $6.4\times10^{-13}\,\mathrm{J}$ and rearrange for $r$.
$E=20.9\,\mathrm{MeV}$.
The original closest distance exceeds the radius, so the projectile turns around outside the nucleus.
At nuclear dimensions, finite charge distribution and nuclear interactions can invalidate the point-charge Coulomb model; neglected recoil is another limitation.

subject: physics-hl
title: Below-threshold illumination
stem: A clean metal has threshold frequency $6.0\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}$. Light of frequency $5.0\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}$ shines on it. Within the single-photon model, what happens when the intensity is doubled?

verification.method: author reasoning, conservation and deterministic numerical checks
verification.notes: Skill family: E2-F1 photon model of photoelectric observations. Variant 1 of 4. Original constructed context/data and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, assumptions and allocations; not independent exam moderation.

options.label: C
options.text: Electrons begin to emerge after a longer delay.

steps.text: Option D. Each photon still has energy $hf<\Phi$. More photons per second do not increase individual photon energy, so no photoelectrons are released in this model.

subject: physics-hl
title: A brighter monochromatic beam
stem: Light well above the threshold frequency illuminates a metal. Its frequency is fixed and its intensity is doubled. All emitted electrons are collected and the emission efficiency stays constant. Which change is predicted?

verification.method: author reasoning, conservation and deterministic numerical checks
verification.notes: Skill family: E2-F1 photon model of photoelectric observations. Variant 2 of 4. Original constructed context/data and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, assumptions and allocations; not independent exam moderation.

options.label: A
options.text: The saturation current is unchanged and the stopping voltage doubles.

options.label: C
options.text: The saturation current doubles and the stopping voltage is unchanged.

options.label: D
options.text: Both saturation current and stopping voltage double.

steps.text: Option C. At fixed frequency, twice the intensity supplies twice as many photons per second, giving twice the electron rate. Maximum electron energy $hf-\Phi$, and therefore stopping voltage, is unchanged.

subject: physics-hl
title: Changing photon energy at fixed photon rate
stem: A metal is illuminated above threshold. The incident photon rate and electron-emission efficiency are held fixed while photon frequency rises. Which change follows?

verification.method: author reasoning, conservation and deterministic numerical checks
verification.notes: Skill family: E2-F1 photon model of photoelectric observations. Variant 3 of 4. Original constructed context/data and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, assumptions and allocations; not independent exam moderation.

options.label: A
options.text: The work function rises in proportion to frequency.

options.label: B
options.text: The stopping voltage rises while the saturation current stays constant.

options.label: C
options.text: The stopping voltage stays constant while the current rises.

options.label: D
options.text: Both stopping voltage and current must fall.

steps.text: Option B. The maximum kinetic energy rises because $K_{\max}=hf-\Phi$. Fixed photon rate and efficiency give the same emitted-electron rate, so the saturation current is constant.

subject: physics-hl
title: Evidence from immediate emission
stem: A very weak beam above a metal's threshold produces photoelectrons without a measurable accumulation delay. Increasing intensity changes the number emitted, not their maximum energy. Which statement explains both observations?

verification.method: author reasoning, conservation and deterministic numerical checks
verification.notes: Skill family: E2-F1 photon model of photoelectric observations. Variant 4 of 4. Original constructed context/data and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, assumptions and allocations; not independent exam moderation.

options.label: A
options.text: An electron can gain the energy of one photon in one interaction.

options.label: B
options.text: An electron must store many wave cycles before escaping.

options.label: C
options.text: Intensity sets the energy of each photon at fixed frequency.

options.label: D
options.text: The metal's work function falls to zero in weak light.

steps.text: Option A. One above-threshold photon can transfer sufficient energy in one interaction. At fixed frequency photon energy is fixed, while intensity controls the number of photons arriving per second.

title: Tuning an electron diffraction beam 1
stem: Electrons start nearly at rest and are accelerated through $36.0\,\mathrm{V}$ before diffracting from a thin target. Use $e=1.60\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$, $m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$, $h=6.63\times10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s}$ and $c=3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. For this fixed apparatus the small-angle ring diameter is proportional to de Broglie wavelength.

verification.method: author reasoning, conservation and deterministic numerical checks
verification.notes: Skill family: E2-F3 electron acceleration and diffraction scaling. Variant 1 of 4. Original constructed context/data and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, assumptions and allocations; not independent exam moderation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the electron speed and de Broglie wavelength using the non-relativistic model.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: The same ring is required to have $0.80$ times its original diameter. Find the new accelerating voltage.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Assess the non-relativistic approximation for the original beam.

steps.text: $eV=\frac12m_ev^2$ and $\lambda=h/(m_ev)$.
$\lambda=2.05\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$.
$D\propto\lambda\propto V^{-1/2}$, so $V_{\rm new}=V_{\rm old}/(D_{\rm new}/D_{\rm old})^2$.
$V_{\rm new}=56.2\,\mathrm{V}$.
This is much less than one, so relativistic corrections are small for the stated precision.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Assess the non-relativistic approximation for the original beam.

steps.text: $eV=\frac12m_ev^2$ and $\lambda=h/(m_ev)$.
$\lambda=1.02\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$.
$D\propto\lambda\propto V^{-1/2}$, so $V_{\rm new}=V_{\rm old}/(D_{\rm new}/D_{\rm old})^2$.
$V_{\rm new}=576\,\mathrm{V}$.
This is much less than one, so relativistic corrections are small for the stated precision.

title: A finite decay interval 1
stem: A model source initially contains $1.2\times10^{6}$ undecayed nuclei of one isotope with decay constant $0.0040\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Each nucleus decays independently. Consider a time interval of $75.0\,\mathrm{s}$. Use the exponential model and report expected populations rather than an exact random outcome.

verification.method: author reasoning, conservation and deterministic numerical checks
verification.notes: Skill family: E3-F3 arbitrary-time decay and finite-interval probability. Variant 1 of 4. Original constructed context/data and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, assumptions and allocations; not independent exam moderation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the expected number of undecayed nuclei and the activity at the end of the interval.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the probability that one initially present nucleus decays during the interval.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Compare the actual expected number of decays with the estimate initial activity multiplied by time. Explain the discrepancy.

steps.text: $N=N_0e^{-\lambda t}$ and $A=\lambda N$.
$N=8.89\times10^{5}$ nuclei.
$A=3.56\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{Bq}$; accept consistent error carried forward from $N$.
Survival probability is $e^{-\lambda t}$, so decay probability is its complement.
Exponential expectation $=3.11\times10^{5}$; $A_0t=3.6\times10^{5}$.
The initial-activity estimate is larger because it assumes the activity remains fixed while the population is actually declining.

subject: physics-hl
title: Interpreting nuclear energy evidence 1
stem: In a simplified nuclear mass dataset, a nucleus has $A=12$, $Z=6$ and nuclear mass $11.997733\,\mathrm{u}$. Use proton mass $1.00728\,\mathrm{u}$, neutron mass $1.00866\,\mathrm{u}$ and $1\,\mathrm{u}c^2=931.5\,\mathrm{MeV}$. These are nuclear masses; electron masses are excluded. A proposed breakup conserves the total proton and neutron numbers and gives fragments with mean binding energy $7.20\,\mathrm{MeV}$ per nucleon. Separately, the schematic beta spectrum shown has endpoint $0.80\,\mathrm{MeV}$.

verification.method: author reasoning, conservation and deterministic numerical checks
verification.notes: Skill family: E3-F4 binding-energy stability and continuous beta evidence. Variant 1 of 4. Original constructed context/data and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, assumptions and allocations; not independent exam moderation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the mass defect and binding energy per nucleon of the original nucleus.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine whether the proposed breakup releases energy.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: In the beta process, an electron emerges with $0.30\,\mathrm{MeV}$. Neglect nuclear recoil and neutrino rest energy. Find the energy carried by the neutrino or antineutrino and explain why the electron spectrum is continuous.

steps.text: $\Delta m=Z m_p+(A-Z)m_n-m_{\rm nucleus}=0.097907\,\mathrm{u}$.
Multiply by $931.5\,\mathrm{MeV\,u^{-1}}$ to obtain total binding energy, then divide by $A$.
$B/A=7.6\,\mathrm{MeV}$.
Reaction energy is final total binding minus initial binding: $Q=12(7.2)-91.2004$ MeV.
$Q=-4.8\,\mathrm{MeV}$; it requires an input of $4.8\,\mathrm{MeV}$.
The more tightly bound original configuration has lower total rest energy than the separated fragments.
The other emitted particle carries approximately $0.8-0.3=0.5\,\mathrm{MeV}$.
The released energy can be shared in different proportions between electron and neutrino/antineutrino; the electron need not take a fixed amount.

title: Interpreting nuclear energy evidence 2
stem: In a simplified nuclear mass dataset, a nucleus has $A=16$, $Z=8$ and nuclear mass $15.990107\,\mathrm{u}$. Use proton mass $1.00728\,\mathrm{u}$, neutron mass $1.00866\,\mathrm{u}$ and $1\,\mathrm{u}c^2=931.5\,\mathrm{MeV}$. These are nuclear masses; electron masses are excluded. A proposed breakup conserves the total proton and neutron numbers and gives fragments with mean binding energy $7.60\,\mathrm{MeV}$ per nucleon. Separately, the schematic beta spectrum shown has endpoint $1.20\,\mathrm{MeV}$.

verification.method: author reasoning, conservation and deterministic numerical checks
verification.notes: Skill family: E3-F4 binding-energy stability and continuous beta evidence. Variant 2 of 4. Original constructed context/data and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, assumptions and allocations; not independent exam moderation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the mass defect and binding energy per nucleon of the original nucleus.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine whether the proposed breakup releases energy.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: In the beta process, an electron emerges with $0.50\,\mathrm{MeV}$. Neglect nuclear recoil and neutrino rest energy. Find the energy carried by the neutrino or antineutrino and explain why the electron spectrum is continuous.

steps.text: $\Delta m=Z m_p+(A-Z)m_n-m_{\rm nucleus}=0.13741\,\mathrm{u}$.
Multiply by $931.5\,\mathrm{MeV\,u^{-1}}$ to obtain total binding energy, then divide by $A$.
$B/A=8\,\mathrm{MeV}$.
Reaction energy is final total binding minus initial binding: $Q=16(7.6)-128$ MeV.
$Q=-6.4\,\mathrm{MeV}$; it requires an input of $6.4\,\mathrm{MeV}$.
The more tightly bound original configuration has lower total rest energy than the separated fragments.
The other emitted particle carries approximately $1.2-0.5=0.7\,\mathrm{MeV}$.
The released energy can be shared in different proportions between electron and neutrino/antineutrino; the electron need not take a fixed amount.

subject: physics-hl
title: Interpreting nuclear energy evidence 4
stem: In a simplified nuclear mass dataset, a nucleus has $A=24$, $Z=12$ and nuclear mass $23.972278\,\mathrm{u}$. Use proton mass $1.00728\,\mathrm{u}$, neutron mass $1.00866\,\mathrm{u}$ and $1\,\mathrm{u}c^2=931.5\,\mathrm{MeV}$. These are nuclear masses; electron masses are excluded. A proposed breakup conserves the total proton and neutron numbers and gives fragments with mean binding energy $8.10\,\mathrm{MeV}$ per nucleon. Separately, the schematic beta spectrum shown has endpoint $2.00\,\mathrm{MeV}$.

verification.method: author reasoning, conservation and deterministic numerical checks
verification.notes: Skill family: E3-F4 binding-energy stability and continuous beta evidence. Variant 4 of 4. Original constructed context/data and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, assumptions and allocations; not independent exam moderation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the mass defect and binding energy per nucleon of the original nucleus.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine whether the proposed breakup releases energy.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: In the beta process, an electron emerges with $1.00\,\mathrm{MeV}$. Neglect nuclear recoil and neutrino rest energy. Find the energy carried by the neutrino or antineutrino and explain why the electron spectrum is continuous.

steps.text: $\Delta m=Z m_p+(A-Z)m_n-m_{\rm nucleus}=0.219\,\mathrm{u}$.
Multiply by $931.5\,\mathrm{MeV\,u^{-1}}$ to obtain total binding energy, then divide by $A$.
$B/A=8.5\,\mathrm{MeV}$.
Reaction energy is final total binding minus initial binding: $Q=24(8.1)-204$ MeV.
$Q=-9.6\,\mathrm{MeV}$; it requires an input of $9.6\,\mathrm{MeV}$.
The more tightly bound original configuration has lower total rest energy than the separated fragments.
The other emitted particle carries approximately $2-1=1\,\mathrm{MeV}$.
The released energy can be shared in different proportions between electron and neutrino/antineutrino; the electron need not take a fixed amount.

subject: physics-hl
title: Reading a decay record 1
stem:
The table gives simulated mean detector count rates from one source plus a constant background of $20\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Geometry and detector efficiency are fixed.

| time / min | detector rate / s⁻¹ |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | 820 |
| 4 | 420 |
| 8 | 220 |
| 12 | 120 |

verification.method: author reasoning, conservation and deterministic numerical checks
verification.notes: Skill family: E3-F5 decay-graph inference and detector calibration. Variant 1 of 4. Original constructed context/data and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, assumptions and allocations; not independent exam moderation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the source half-life after allowing for background.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Predict the mean detector rate at $16\,\mathrm{min}$.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why a real short count would not be expected to equal the model mean exactly.

steps.text: The initial net rate is $800\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$; compare net rates rather than raw detector readings.
Successive net rates halve every $4\,\mathrm{min}$, so this is the half-life.
Reduce the initial source contribution through four half-lives and restore background.
Individual decays and detections are random, so finite counts fluctuate statistically around the mean.

title: Reading a decay record 2
stem:
The table gives simulated mean detector count rates from one source plus a constant background of $30\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Geometry and detector efficiency are fixed.

| time / min | detector rate / s⁻¹ |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | 990 |
| 6 | 510 |
| 12 | 270 |
| 18 | 150 |

verification.method: author reasoning, conservation and deterministic numerical checks
verification.notes: Skill family: E3-F5 decay-graph inference and detector calibration. Variant 2 of 4. Original constructed context/data and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, assumptions and allocations; not independent exam moderation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the source half-life after allowing for background.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Predict the mean detector rate at $24\,\mathrm{min}$.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why a real short count would not be expected to equal the model mean exactly.

steps.text: The initial net rate is $960\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$; compare net rates rather than raw detector readings.
Successive net rates halve every $6\,\mathrm{min}$, so this is the half-life.
Reduce the initial source contribution through four half-lives and restore background.
Individual decays and detections are random, so finite counts fluctuate statistically around the mean.

title: Reading a decay record 3
stem:
Background has already been subtracted from a source's detected count rate $r$. The table gives constructed values of $\ln[r/(1\,\mathrm{s^{-1}})]$. The detector records a constant fraction $0.250$ of decays.

| time / s | ln[r / (1 s⁻¹)] |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | 5.9915 |
| 100 | 5.6715 |
| 200 | 5.3515 |
| 300 | 5.0315 |
| 400 | 4.7115 |

verification.method: author reasoning, conservation and deterministic numerical checks
verification.notes: Skill family: E3-F5 decay-graph inference and detector calibration. Variant 3 of 4. Original constructed context/data and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, assumptions and allocations; not independent exam moderation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the decay constant and half-life.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Estimate the initial number of undecayed nuclei.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why taking logarithms before subtracting background would spoil this linear model.

steps.text: From $\ln r=\ln r_0-\lambda t$, the negative gradient is $\lambda$.
$\lambda=0.0032\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $t_{1/2}=\ln2/\lambda=217\,\mathrm{s}$. Accept 1% from displayed data.
Exponentiate the intercept to find $r_0\approx400\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$; $r_0=\epsilon\lambda N_0$.
$N_0=5\times10^{5}$ nuclei; allow consistent ECF from the fitted decay constant.
The raw rate is $r_0e^{-\lambda t}+b$. The logarithm of this sum is not a straight line in time; it flattens towards the background level.

title: Reading a decay record 4
stem: A source has half-life $12.0\,\mathrm{h}$. At preparation its background-corrected detected rate was $600\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ with detection efficiency $0.250$. At a later measurement the efficiency is $0.200$, the raw detector rate is $108\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and the background is $12.0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The source contains one isotope and has not lost material.

verification.method: author reasoning, conservation and deterministic numerical checks
verification.notes: Skill family: E3-F5 decay-graph inference and detector calibration. Variant 4 of 4. Original constructed context/data and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, assumptions and allocations; not independent exam moderation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the original and later source activities.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the source's age at the later measurement.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A student divides the later net detector rate by the original net detector rate without correcting efficiencies. Explain the direction of the age error.

steps.text: Correct the later rate for background and use $A=r/\epsilon$ at each measurement.
$A_0=2400\,\mathrm{Bq}$ and $A=480\,\mathrm{Bq}$.
$A/A_0=0.200=e^{-\lambda t}$ with $\lambda=\ln2/12.0\,\mathrm{h^{-1}}$.
$t=27.9\,\mathrm{h}$; accept consistent ECF from the activity ratio.
The lower later efficiency makes this detected-rate ratio smaller than the true activity ratio.
A smaller surviving fraction would imply too many half-lives, so the calculated age would be too large.

title: The role of moderator
stem: A reactor component reduces the speed of neutrons mainly through collisions. What is its intended function?

verification.method: author reasoning, conservation and deterministic numerical checks
verification.notes: Skill family: E4-F1 distinct reactor component functions. Variant 1 of 4. Original constructed context/data and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, assumptions and allocations; not independent exam moderation.

options.label: A
options.text: To absorb every neutron so no further fission can occur.

options.label: B
options.text: To convert thermal energy directly into electrical energy.

options.label: C
options.text: To make the nuclei's proton numbers decrease.

options.label: D
options.text: To increase the chance that suitable slower neutrons induce fission in the fuel.

steps.text: Option D. The moderator slows neutrons by collisions; in the stated thermal-reactor context, slower neutrons have a greater probability of causing fission in the selected fuel.

options.label: A
options.text: The rods raise the binding energy of every fuel nucleus.

options.label: B
options.text: The rods immediately remove all radioactive decay products.

options.label: C
options.text: Neutron absorption reduces the number available to cause subsequent fissions.

options.label: D
options.text: Neutrons gain kinetic energy from the rods until they stop fissioning.

steps.text: Option C. Control rods absorb neutrons. Fewer neutrons remain to initiate the next generation of fissions, reducing the multiplication factor.

title: Balancing a fission channel 1
stem: Consider the possible induced-fission channel $^{235}_{92}\mathrm{U}+^1_0\mathrm{n}\rightarrow ^{141}_{56}\mathrm{Ba}+^{92}_{36}\mathrm{Kr}+k\,^1_0\mathrm{n}$. No other particles carrying nucleon number are emitted. What is $k$?

verification.method: author reasoning, conservation and deterministic numerical checks
verification.notes: Skill family: E4-F2 fission nucleon and charge conservation. Variant 1 of 4. Original constructed context/data and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, assumptions and allocations; not independent exam moderation.

steps.text: Option D. The initial nucleon number is $235+1=236$. The fragments contain $141+92=233$ nucleons, leaving $k=3$ neutrons. Proton number is also conserved because $56+36=92$.

title: Energy accounting for a reactor model 1
stem: The summed masses before one fission are $236.052600\,\mathrm{u}$ and after it are $235.872600\,\mathrm{u}$. The sums include all emitted neutrons and equal numbers of atomic electrons on both sides, so electron masses cancel. The average thermal power is $150\,\mathrm{MW}$ and electrical efficiency is $0.30$. Assume all reaction energy becomes heat, each fission consumes one fuel nucleus of mass $235\,\mathrm{u}$, and no other fuel losses occur. Use $1\,\mathrm{u}c^2=931.5\,\mathrm{MeV}$, $1\,\mathrm{MeV}=1.60\times10^{-13}\,\mathrm{J}$ and $1\,\mathrm{u}=1.66\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$.

parts.label: c

steps.text: $k=\nu(1-\ell)p$.
Because $k>1$, the expected number of fissions increases from generation to generation.
Apply the same factor twenty times: $N_{20}/N_0=k^{20}$.

Neutron absorption in control rods reduces the number available for further fissions; a moderator's principal role is slowing, not absorbing, neutrons.

subject: physics-hl
title: Following a model neutron population 4
stem: In a simplified thermal-reactor model each fission emits on average $2.80$ neutrons. A fraction $0.18$ is lost before it can interact with fuel. Each remaining neutron has probability $0.440$ of inducing the next fission. Ignore the time taken by a generation and all feedback. This is an average population model, not an engineering design.

verification.method: author reasoning, conservation and deterministic numerical checks
verification.notes: Skill family: E4-F4 neutron generations and controlled multiplication. Variant 4 of 4. Original constructed context/data and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, assumptions and allocations; not independent exam moderation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the expected multiplication factor k, defined as next-generation fissions divided by current-generation fissions. Classify the trend.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the ratio of the twentieth-generation fission count to the initial count.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Keeping neutron production and losses fixed, find the inducing probability required for a steady expected count. Explain the relevant role of control rods.

steps.text: $k=\nu(1-\ell)p$.
Because $k>1$, the expected number of fissions increases from generation to generation.
Apply the same factor twenty times: $N_{20}/N_0=k^{20}$.
Ratio $=1.23$; allow consistent ECF from $k$.
Set $k=1$, giving $p_{\rm steady}=1/[\nu(1-\ell)]$.
Neutron absorption in control rods reduces the number available for further fissions; a moderator's principal role is slowing, not absorbing, neutrons.

title: Cooling after shutdown 1
stem:
A constructed dataset models heat from one dominant radioactive fission product after a reactor is shut down. Heat power is proportional to its activity; no new nuclei of this product are formed.

| time / years | heat power / W |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | 640.0 |
| 2 | 320.0 |
| 4 | 160.0 |
| 6 | 80.0 |

A particular thermal calculation asks when this component's heat output first reaches $40\,\mathrm{W}$.

steps.text: Successive powers halve, indicating that the activity halves over each equal time interval.
Half-life $=2\,\mathrm{years}$.

Heat power alone does not specify radiation type, activity, exposure pathways or containment; radioactive material may remain after its heat output has fallen.

verification.method: author reasoning, conservation and deterministic numerical checks
verification.notes: Skill family: E4-F5 fission-product decay-heat interpretation. Variant 3 of 4. Original constructed context/data and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, assumptions and allocations; not independent exam moderation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the fractional heat remaining over the first and last three-year intervals.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why one fixed half-life cannot describe all of these total-power values.

parts.label: c

steps.text: Divide the later power by the earlier power for each interval.
First interval: $0.551$; last interval: $0.701$.

The short-lived contribution becomes less important, leaving a larger relative contribution from the slower-decaying component.
After the short-lived component becomes negligible, the total increasingly follows the longer-lived component's slower decline.

title: Cooling after shutdown 4
stem: A waste model contains two independent products. Initially S has activity $8.0\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{Bq}$ and deposits on average $0.80\,\mathrm{MeV}$ as heat per decay; L has activity $3.0\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{Bq}$ and deposits $2.4\,\mathrm{MeV}$ per decay. Their half-lives are $2.0\,\mathrm{years}$ and $8.0\,\mathrm{years}$ respectively. Neither feeds the other. The quoted deposited energies already exclude escaping energy. Use $1\,\mathrm{MeV}=1.60\times10^{-13}\,\mathrm{J}$.

verification.method: author reasoning, conservation and deterministic numerical checks
verification.notes: Skill family: E4-F5 fission-product decay-heat interpretation. Variant 4 of 4. Original constructed context/data and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, assumptions and allocations; not independent exam moderation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find each product's initial heat power and the total.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the total heat power eight years later and its fraction of the initial power.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the claim that the component with greater activity must produce more heat and that the total power must halve every eight years.

steps.text: Power is activity times deposited energy per decay.
$P_S=102\,\mathrm{W}$, $P_L=115\,\mathrm{W}$; total $=218\,\mathrm{W}$.
S undergoes four half-lives and L undergoes one; apply the factors separately before adding.
Remaining fraction $=0.294$; allow consistent ECF.
Heat depends on energy deposited per decay as well as activity; L initially produces more heat despite its lower activity.
The total combines different decay rates, so it has no single fixed half-life during the mixed stage.

title: Energy in light-nucleus fusion 1
stem: Consider the fusion channel $^2_1\mathrm{H}+^3_1\mathrm{H}\rightarrow{}^4_2\mathrm{He}+{}^1_0\mathrm{n}$. steps.text: Divide by the solar relation to obtain $R/R_\odot=\sqrt{L/L_\odot}(T_\odot/T)^2$.

verification.method: author reasoning, conservation and deterministic numerical checks
verification.notes: Skill family: E5-F3 HR positions and stellar radius inference. Variant 4 of 4. Original constructed context/data and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, assumptions and allocations; not independent exam moderation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find each stellar radius in units of the solar radius.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how stars with the same luminosity can occupy these different HR positions.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Compare X with main-sequence stars of similar surface temperature and identify its broad region on the diagram.

steps.text: Divide by the solar relation to obtain $R/R_\odot=\sqrt{L/L_\odot}(T_\odot/T)^2$.
X: $R_X=20.6R_\odot$.
Y: $R_Y=1.29R_\odot$.
The cooler star emits less energy per unit surface area, so a larger surface area compensates.
Temperature distinguishes their horizontal positions, while equal luminosity places them at the same vertical position.
X is much more luminous and larger than main-sequence stars of similar temperature, placing it in the giant region above the main sequence.

title: A model stellar lifetime 1
stem: A main-sequence star has mass $1.0M_\odot$ and constant model luminosity $1.0L_\odot$. Only $0.10$ of its mass participates in core hydrogen burning; $0.70$ of that participating mass is hydrogen. Fusion converts $0.0070$ of the consumed hydrogen mass into released energy. Take $M_\odot=2.00\times10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}$, $L_\odot=3.80\times10^{26}\,\mathrm{W}$, $c=3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and one year as $3.156\times10^7\,\mathrm{s}$. Assume all the released energy contributes to the luminosity.

verification.method: author reasoning, conservation and deterministic numerical checks
verification.notes: Skill family: E5-F4 fusion fuel budgets and stellar evolution. Variant 1 of 4. Original constructed context/data and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, assumptions and allocations; not independent exam moderation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Estimate the available fusion energy and the duration of core hydrogen burning.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: A comparison star has twice the mass and ten times the luminosity, with the same usable fractions. Compare its model lifetime.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why a sufficiently hot stellar core can sustain fusion and how a star is supported during a stable stage.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: In the stated low-mass evolutionary scenario, core hydrogen is exhausted and outer layers are eventually ejected without core collapse. Name the remnant and describe its subsequent energy source.

steps.text: Available energy $E=(0.10)(0.70)(0.0070)Mc^2$.
Use $t=E/L$ and convert seconds to years.
$t\approx7.35\times10^{9}\,\mathrm{years}$. Accept rounding with the supplied year conversion.
Usable fuel energy scales with mass, so $t'/t=2/10$.
Its lifetime is 0.20 times as long: a greater fuel supply is outweighed by a much greater rate of energy release.
High temperature supplies large particle kinetic energies, increasing the chance of close nuclear encounters despite electric repulsion.
An outward pressure gradient, from thermal gas and/or radiation pressure, balances inward gravitational force.
The remnant is a white dwarf.
It cools by radiating stored internal energy; it has no sustained core fusion.

title: Interpreting a stellar observation 3
stem: A simulated stellar dataset gives annual parallax $0.0500$ arcseconds, received energy flux $3.00\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, and a blackbody spectral peak at $500\,\mathrm{nm}$. Neglect absorption and use $d/\mathrm{pc}=1/(p/\mathrm{arcsec})$, $1\,\mathrm{pc}=3.09\times10^{16}\,\mathrm{m}$, $\lambda_{\max}T=2.90\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m\,K}$ and $\sigma=5.67\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-4}}$.

verification.method: author reasoning, conservation and deterministic numerical checks
verification.notes: Skill family: E5-F5 stellar observation inversion and parallax calibration. Variant 3 of 4. Original constructed context/data and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, assumptions and allocations; not independent exam moderation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the distance and surface temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Estimate the luminosity and stellar radius.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the effect of unrecognized absorption on the radius estimate if parallax and temperature remain correct.

steps.text: $d=20\,\mathrm{pc}=6.18\times10^{17}\,\mathrm{m}$.
Apply Wien's relation with the wavelength in metres.
$T=5.8\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{K}$.
$L=4\pi d^2b$, then $R=\sqrt{L/(4\pi\sigma T^4)}$.
$R=1.34\times10^{9}\,\mathrm{m}$. Accept consistent ECF from distance or temperature.
Absorption reduces the received flux, so inferred luminosity is too small; at fixed temperature the inferred radius is also too small.

title: Interpreting a stellar observation 4
stem:
A star's measured displacement is modelled by $x(t)=\mu t+p\sin(2\pi t)$, where $t$ is time in years, $\mu$ is steady proper motion in arcseconds per year and $p$ is annual parallax in arcseconds. The annual phase is known. The constructed measurements below are rounded to the shown precision.

| t / years | x / arcsec |
| --- | --- |
| 0.00 | 0.000 |
| 0.25 | 0.070 |
| 0.50 | 0.060 |
| 0.75 | 0.050 |
| 1.00 | 0.120 |

Its received flux is $2.00\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$. Use $d/\mathrm{pc}=1/(p/\mathrm{arcsec})$ and $1\,\mathrm{pc}=3.09\times10^{16}\,\mathrm{m}$. Neglect absorption.

verification.method: author reasoning, conservation and deterministic numerical checks
verification.notes: Skill family: E5-F5 stellar observation inversion and parallax calibration. Variant 4 of 4. Original constructed context/data and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, assumptions and allocations; not independent exam moderation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine proper motion and annual parallax from the measurements.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the distance and luminosity.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A student uses half the difference between the positions at 0.25 and 0.75 years as p, without removing proper motion. Quantify the distance error.

steps.text: At zero and one year the sinusoidal term is zero; the endpoint difference gives the steady drift.
$\mu=0.120\,\mathrm{arcsec\,year^{-1}}$.
At $t=0.25$ subtract $\mu t=0.030$ arcsec from $x=0.070$ arcsec.
$p=0.0400$ arcsec.
Use the corrected parallax to find distance, then $L=4\pi d^2b$.
$d=25\,\mathrm{pc}$ and $L=1.5\times10^{27}\,\mathrm{W}$. Accept ECF from the inferred parallax.
This gives $p_{\rm wrong}=(0.070-0.050)/2=0.0100$ arcsec, hence $d_{\rm wrong}=100\,\mathrm{pc}$.
The distance is four times the correct value because the steady drift partly cancels the annual displacement difference.

subject: physics-hl
title: Emission from a model atom
stem:
A model atom has the three bound energy levels shown. Ignore all other levels. Use $1\,\mathrm{eV}=1.60\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$, $h=6.63\times10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s}$ and $c=3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

Give calculated numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the photon energy in joules for a transition from level 3 to level 2.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the frequency and wavelength of that photon.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: List all possible downward-transition photon energies in eV and hence the number of distinct emission lines.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Identify the transition with the longest wavelength and find its wavelength.

steps.text: Subtract the lower energy from the upper energy and convert eV to J.
Use $E=hf$ and $c=f\lambda$.
$f=7.24\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}$.
$\lambda=4.14\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{m}$.
Photon energies are $2.00$, $3.00$ and $5.00\,\mathrm{eV}$.
These three energy differences are distinct, so there are three distinct lines.
The smallest energy difference gives the longest wavelength: level 2 to level 1.
$\lambda_\mathrm{max}=6.22\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{m}$.

verification.method: Author numerical, dimensional and model-consistency checks; independent review recorded separately
verification.notes: Levels specified independently rather than Bohr model; all3positivegaps=[2.0, 3.0, 5.0]; level3→2E=4.7999999999999995e-19,frequency=723981900452488.6; maxλ=6.215625e-07. SL photon/atomic transitions.

subject: physics-hl
title: Background-corrected decay observations
stem:
A detector counts radiation for the same short interval at each listed time. The following counts are simulated mean values, so statistical scatter is omitted. An independent background measurement gives $20$ counts per measurement interval. Detector geometry and efficiency are unchanged; each measurement interval is short compared with the half-life.

| Elapsed time / min | Total counts per interval |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | 660.0 |
| 6 | 340.0 |
| 12 | 180.0 |
| 18 | 100.0 |



Give calculated numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the initial count due to the source alone.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the half-life and support your answer using two successive intervals.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Predict the total detector count per interval at elapsed time $24\,\mathrm{min}$.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain why a single real measurement could differ from this prediction.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Explain whether doubling the initial amount of this isotope changes its half-life.

steps.text: Subtract the background from the total count.
$640$ counts per interval.
After background subtraction, the count halves over each of the first two equal time intervals.
The source has undergone four half-lives, so its contribution is one sixteenth of the initial value.
Total $=60.0$ counts per interval, including background.
Radioactive decay is random, so counts fluctuate statistically even with stable apparatus.
It does not: half-life is a property of the isotope. The expected source count rate doubles, but the fractional decay in one half-life remains the same.

subject: physics-hl
title: An idealized fission power calculation
stem:
An idealized reactor supplies electrical power $4.00\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{W}$ at efficiency $0.30$. Each fission releases $190\,\mathrm{MeV}$ as recoverable thermal energy. Assume all this thermal energy is transferred to the power cycle and the output is steady. One fuel nucleus has mass $3.90\times10^{-25}\,\mathrm{kg}$ and undergoes one fission. Use $1\,\mathrm{eV}=1.60\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$ and $c=3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

Give calculated numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the required thermal power.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the number of fissions per second.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the mass equivalent of the energy released in one fission.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Calculate the mass of fuel nuclei that undergo fission in one day.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Explain one condition needed to sustain a controlled fission chain reaction.

steps.text: $P_\mathrm{thermal}=P_\mathrm{electrical}/\eta$.
Convert the energy per fission from MeV to J.
Divide thermal energy required per second by energy per fission.
$\Delta m=E/c^2$.
$\Delta m=3.38\times10^{-28}\,\mathrm{kg}$.
Multiply fissions per second by 86400 s and by the supplied mass per nucleus.
$1.48\,\mathrm{kg}$.
On average one neutron from each fission must cause a further fission; control rods can absorb excess neutrons to keep the reaction rate steady.

verification.method: Author numerical, dimensional and model-consistency checks; independent review recorded separately
verification.notes: Inputthermalpower1333333333.3333335;recoverableEfission3.04e-11;rate4.385964912280702e+19; massdefect3.377777777777778e-28;fuelconsumed1.4778947368421054kg/day. Distinguishes fuelmass from smallmassdefect.

subject: physics-hl
title: Inferring stellar properties from radiation
stem:
A star is modelled as an isotropically radiating spherical black body. Its observed wavelength of maximum emission is $5.8e-07\,\mathrm{m}$, and the received bolometric intensity is $2.00\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$ at distance $2.00\times10^{17}\,\mathrm{m}$. Neglect interstellar absorption and spectral shifts. Use Wien constant $2.90\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m\,K}$ and $\sigma=5.67\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}K^{-4}}$.

Give calculated numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the surface temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the luminosity.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the stellar radius.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A second black-body star has the same radius and twice the surface temperature. Compare the luminosities.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Explain how a stable star can maintain a roughly constant radius.

steps.text: Use $\lambda_\mathrm{max}T=b$.
Use $L=4\pi R^2\sigma T^4$.
At fixed radius luminosity is proportional to the fourth power of temperature.
The second star has 16 times the luminosity.
The inward gravitational tendency is balanced by the outward effect of thermal and radiation pressure, maintaining hydrostatic equilibrium.

verification.method: Author numerical, dimensional and model-consistency checks; independent review recorded separately
verification.notes: Displayed peak9significantdigits determines T=5000.0, unroundedtarget5000;inverse-squareL=1.0053096491487339e+26;radius475131096.7331989; unitconsistencyverified. Thermal/radiationpressure correctedguidewording.

subject: physics-hl
title: Identifying a mixed radioactive source
stem:
A source emits a mixture of alpha, beta-minus and gamma radiation. A detector gives these simulated mean counts in equal intervals. Background is $15$ counts per interval. For this idealized test, paper stops all alpha and no beta or gamma; aluminium stops all beta and no gamma. The lead absorbs part of the remaining gamma radiation. Geometry and detector response are unchanged.

| Absorber arrangement | Total counts per interval |
| --- | --- |
| No absorber | 815 |
| Thin paper | 615.0 |
| Several millimetres of aluminium | 215.0 |
| Aluminium plus thick lead | 55.0 |



Give calculated numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use the measurements to find the separate alpha, beta and gamma count contributions before absorbers.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the fraction of gamma radiation transmitted by the thick lead.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Compare the ionizing ability and penetration of alpha and gamma radiation.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: State why these detected contributions do not directly give the fractions of decays of each type in the source.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Explain why repeating and averaging the measurements improves this comparison.

steps.text: Subtract background for the gamma contribution and use successive differences for beta and alpha.
Alpha $200$, beta $400$, gamma $200$ counts per interval.
Subtract the background from both gamma-only readings before taking their ratio.
Transmitted fraction $0.200$.
Alpha is more strongly ionizing over a short path and is less penetrating.
Gamma is less strongly ionizing locally and is much more penetrating.
Detection efficiencies, emission directions and absorption before detection can differ between radiation types, so detected count fractions need not equal decay fractions.
It reduces the influence of random counting fluctuations, although it does not remove a systematic error in background or detector efficiency.

verification.method: Author numerical, dimensional and model-consistency checks; independent review recorded separately
verification.notes: Exactsimulatedcomponentsalpha200.0,beta400.0,gamma200.0,background15; leadtransmission0.2 afterbackground. No unsupportedinferenceofactivityfractions.

title: Identifying a mixed radioactive source
stem:
A source emits a mixture of alpha, beta-minus and gamma radiation. A detector gives these simulated mean counts in equal intervals. Background is $24$ counts per interval. For this idealized test, paper stops all alpha and no beta or gamma; aluminium stops all beta and no gamma. The lead absorbs part of the remaining gamma radiation. Geometry and detector response are unchanged.

| Absorber arrangement | Total counts per interval |
| --- | --- |
| No absorber | 1064 |
| Thin paper | 804.0 |
| Several millimetres of aluminium | 284.0 |
| Aluminium plus thick lead | 76.0 |



Give calculated numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use the measurements to find the separate alpha, beta and gamma count contributions before absorbers.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the fraction of gamma radiation transmitted by the thick lead.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Compare the ionizing ability and penetration of alpha and gamma radiation.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: State why these detected contributions do not directly give the fractions of decays of each type in the source.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Explain why repeating and averaging the measurements improves this comparison.

steps.text: Subtract background for the gamma contribution and use successive differences for beta and alpha.
Alpha $260$, beta $520$, gamma $260$ counts per interval.
Subtract the background from both gamma-only readings before taking their ratio.
Transmitted fraction $0.200$.
Alpha is more strongly ionizing over a short path and is less penetrating.
Gamma is less strongly ionizing locally and is much more penetrating.
Detection efficiencies, emission directions and absorption before detection can differ between radiation types, so detected count fractions need not equal decay fractions.
It reduces the influence of random counting fluctuations, although it does not remove a systematic error in background or detector efficiency.
